benevolent

/buh-NEV-uh-luhnt/ - the stress falls on NEV · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Benevolent means kind and inclined to do good for others.

Ship's logs describe a benevolent captain who let stowaways work off their passage instead of handing them over at the next port.

Example

The hardware store on Fifth has a second, unwritten price list, kept by its benevolent owner. Mrs. Delgado charges full price for paint and nails, then sends her nephew, free of charge, to rehang doors for customers too old to climb ladders. She slips seed packets into the bags of anyone who mentions a garden and never rings them up.

Benevolent is the exact word for Mrs. Delgado, because it means kind and inclined to do good for others — the inclination is the point. She does not wait to be asked; doing good is her standing policy. Nice is far weaker: a nice shopkeeper smiles at you, while a benevolent one is already looking for something to do for you.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

kindly: Kindly is warmth of manner — a kindly voice, a kindly smile, gentleness in how someone treats you moment to moment. Benevolent reaches past manner to a standing drive: a benevolent person is already looking for good to do, and the record of deeds, not the tone, is the proof.

goodhearted: Goodhearted says a person's nature is warm and well-intentioned, and it stays true even when no help ever gets given — good instincts, kind wishes. Benevolent adds the motor: an inclination that keeps turning into actual good done for others, a pattern anyone can point to.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

spiteful: eager to see others hurt

coldhearted: unmoved by anyone's need

Where it sits · how much good actually gets done

well-meaning → benevolent → saintly

well-meaning vs. benevolent: Well-meaning is weaker than benevolent: a well-meaning neighbor merely intends good, even if he never acts, while a benevolent one actually does good for others again and again.

saintly vs. benevolent: Saintly goes further than benevolent — it points to goodness past everyday human reach, while benevolent people do real good on an everyday scale.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — bene: well, good (Latin)

Root — vol: to wish, to will (Latin velle)

Suffix — -ent: adjective ending: inclined to

Put it together: Bene (well) + vol (to wish) + -ent = wishing others well. Latin benevolens meant exactly that, and English keeps both pieces busy elsewhere: the same bene sits in benefactor, this unit's giver, and the same vol sits in volunteer — someone whose own will, not an order, brings them to the work.

Use the root in a new word: volunteer: No one assigned her the dawn cleanup shift - she took it of her own volition.

Word Choice

warm / formal

Benevolent describes the disposition — kindness with a motor in it. Its unit-mates divide the scene: the benefactor is the person a cause thanks, while largess and munificence name the giving itself. Call a ruler, an employer, or a stranger benevolent when their kindness shows a pattern, not a single warm moment.
